title: The Second Klan and Those Who Exposed It
bigQuestion: How did the 1920s Klan grow so large, and how did reporters, courts and ordinary people break its hold?

story.title: Names in the Morning Paper
story.kicker: In 1922, a Chicago weekly called Tolerance prints the names of people it says belong to the Klan.
paragraphs: It is 1922 in Chicago. The Ku Klux Klan has come north, and it has come to the city. By one count it will soon have about 50,000 members in the Chicago area, more than any other American city. Members meet in rented halls and in fields at the edge of town. Most keep their membership secret from neighbors and bosses.

A new group, the American Unity League, has decided to fight that secrecy. Most of its members are Catholic. The Klan attacks Catholics, Jews, Black Americans and immigrants. The League's weapon is a weekly paper called Tolerance. Week after week, it prints the names of people it says are Klan members. It adds their addresses and their jobs.

Picture a kitchen table on a weekday morning. A family opens the paper. The father runs his finger down a long column of names. There is a name he knows from the corner store. There is a name from his own street. The family looks out the window at the houses nearby, and nothing looks quite the same.

For a member, being named could cost friends, customers or a job. For a person named by mistake, the cost could be the same. Tolerance had pulled away the Klan's hood of secrecy, just as the Klan's targets hoped. It had also raised a hard question. When is it right to publish a list of names, and what if the list is wrong?
story.think: Was printing the names of Klan members a fair way to fight a secret hate group? What would you want to know before deciding?

lessons.title: The Film and the Mountain
lessons.mainIdea: A 1915 film glorified the first Klan, and that same year William J. Simmons launched a second Klan on Stone Mountain, Georgia.
reading: On February 8, 1915, a long silent film opened in Los Angeles. It was first called The Clansman and was soon renamed The Birth of a Nation. Director D. W. Griffith based it on a novel by Thomas Dixon. The film was *propaganda*. It showed Black citizens of the Reconstruction South as dangers and showed the Klan as heroes who saved the South.

The *NAACP*, a civil rights group founded in 1909, organized protests. Its members picketed theaters and asked cities to ban the film or cut its worst scenes. The film drew huge crowds anyway. It taught millions of viewers a false version of the history you studied in the last chapter.

On Thanksgiving night, November 25, 1915, William J. Simmons led a small group up Stone Mountain, near Atlanta, Georgia. They burned a cross and declared a new Ku Klux Klan. Simmons won a state charter in early December. The film opened in Atlanta on December 6, and he used its fame to recruit. This *revival* is called the second Klan.

words.d: messages made to push people toward a belief, often by twisting the truth
the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, a civil rights group founded in 1909
bringing something back after it had ended

look.title: Outside the Theater, 1915
look.text: Picture a crowd outside a theater in 1915. Many people buy tickets eagerly. Near the door, a small group holds signs asking the city to stop the film. The poster on the wall shows a hooded rider on a horse, painted as a hero.
look.prompt: What might the ticket buyers believe they are about to learn? What were the protesters trying to protect?

check.why: The reading says Simmons led a group up Stone Mountain on Thanksgiving night, November 25, 1915.

check.q: How did the NAACP respond to The Birth of a Nation?
choices: It paid to make the film
It organized protests and asked cities to ban it
check.why: The reading says the NAACP picketed theaters and asked cities to ban the film or cut its worst scenes.

check.q: What is propaganda?
choices: Messages that push a belief, often by twisting the truth
check.why: The reading calls the film propaganda, defined as messages made to push a belief, often by twisting the truth.

lessons.title: Selling a Secret Order
lessons.mainIdea: From 1920, paid recruiters sold Klan membership like a product, using the familiar look of fraternal lodges.
reading: At first the new Klan grew slowly. In 1920, Simmons hired two *publicists*, Edward Young Clarke and Mary Elizabeth Tyler. A publicist is someone paid to spread the word about a person or product. Their firm was called the Southern Publicity Association. They treated the Klan like a product to sell. Recruiters called Kleagles fanned out across the country.

Each new member paid a $10 joining fee. The recruiter kept part of it as a *commission*, a share of a sale paid to the seller. The rest moved up to leaders above him. Members also bought robes and other goods from the organization. Money flowed upward from every new recruit, which gave recruiters a strong reason to sign up as many people as they could.

The Klan copied the look of *fraternal* lodges, which are brotherhood clubs with rituals. It had a ritual book, passwords and grand titles. Millions of Americans already belonged to lodges and found that style familiar. But the second Klan used the lodge form to spread hatred. Its recruiters told each town it would defend the town against whatever that town feared.

words.d: people paid to spread the word about a person, group or product
a share of a sale paid to the person who made the sale
having to do with a brotherhood or club whose members call each other brothers

look.title: A Recruiter's Pitch
look.text: Imagine a recruiter in 1922 visiting a small-town lodge hall. He does not start with violence. He talks about flag, church and protecting the community. He offers a secret handshake, a robe and the warm feeling of belonging. At the very end, he mentions the $10 fee.
look.prompt: What was the recruiter really selling? Why might a harmful group hide its goals behind friendly words?

choices: Rowland Thomas and Herbert Bayard Swope

Ida B. Wells and Stetson Kennedy

check.why: The reading says each new member paid a $10 joining fee.

choices: A share of a sale paid to the seller
check.why: The reading defines a commission as a share of a sale paid to the seller, which is how recruiters earned money.

lessons.title: Targets and Territory
lessons.mainIdea: The second Klan attacked Black Americans, Catholics, Jews and immigrants, and it was strong in Northern cities like Chicago.
reading: The second Klan targeted more groups than the first. It attacked Black Americans, as before. It also attacked Catholics, Jews and immigrants, especially from southern and eastern Europe. This was *nativism*, the belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers. The Klan also claimed to defend *Prohibition*, the national ban on alcohol, and to police people's private lives.

Many people picture the 1920s Klan as a rural Southern group. The record says otherwise. It was strong in the North and West, in states like Indiana, Oregon, Colorado and Michigan. It was strong in cities like Indianapolis, Detroit, Denver and Chicago. The Encyclopedia of Chicago counts about 50,000 members in the Chicago area, the largest city membership in the nation.

How big was the Klan in all? No reliable national lists survive, so historians must *estimate*. Their estimates run from about 2 million to more than 5 million members at the peak in the mid-1920s. On August 8, 1925, tens of thousands of members marched down Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C. Many marched with their faces uncovered.

words.d: the belief that people born in a country deserve more rights than newcomers
the national ban on making and selling alcohol, from 1920 to 1933
to make a careful guess about a number when an exact count is not possible

choices: In the North and West, including Indiana and Chicago

check.why: The reading says no reliable national lists survive, so historians must estimate.

lessons.title: The World's Exposé
lessons.mainIdea: The New York World's 1921 exposé revealed the Klan's money and violence, won a Pulitzer Prize, and also helped the Klan grow.
reading: On September 6, 1921, the New York World began a series about the Klan. It ran for 21 days in a row. Editor Herbert Bayard Swope oversaw the project. Reporter Rowland Thomas did much of the digging. Other newspapers across the country also printed the series, so readers far beyond New York saw it.

An *exposé* is a report that reveals hidden wrongdoing. The World printed the Klan's own membership forms. It showed how money from fees moved up to the leaders. It listed violent attacks linked to Klan members, including floggings and tar-and-featherings. The paper won the 1922 *Pulitzer Prize* for Public Service.

Then came a surprise. After the series, Klan membership grew. Klan leaders themselves said the exposé had helped them. For some readers, the stories worked like free advertising. This is a real puzzle for anyone fighting hate. Attention can expose a group, and it can also spread its message. Growth was an *unintended consequence* of the World's work.

words.d: a report that reveals hidden wrongdoing
a top American award for journalism, given each year since 1917
a result that no one planned or wanted

look.title: Two Readers, One Series
look.text: Reader A finishes the World series and writes to her member of Congress, asking for an investigation. Reader B finishes the same series and mails in an application to join the Klan. Both read the same facts about fees, secrets and violence.
look.prompt: Why might the same facts push two readers in opposite directions? What could reporters do to lower the chance of Reader B's reaction?

choices: A report that reveals hidden wrongdoing
check.why: The reading defines an exposé as a report that reveals hidden wrongdoing.

check.q: What award did the World win for the series?
choices: The Pulitzer Prize for Public Service
check.why: The reading says the World won the 1922 Pulitzer Prize for Public Service.

check.q: What unintended consequence followed the exposé?
choices: The World went out of business
check.why: The reading says Klan membership grew after the series, and Klan leaders said the exposé helped them.

lessons.title: The Hearing in Congress
lessons.mainIdea: In 1921 a House committee questioned Simmons, who called the Klan a patriotic fraternal order, but Congress passed no law.
reading: The exposé pushed Congress to act. On October 11, 1921, the House Committee on Rules opened *hearings* on the Klan. A hearing is a meeting where lawmakers question witnesses to gather facts. Reporters from the World and critics of the Klan gave evidence about what they had found.

William J. Simmons testified too. He presented the Klan as a patriotic, law-abiding *fraternal order*, a brotherhood like many other lodges. He denied that the Klan as an organization had ordered the violence in the newspapers. His performance was calm and confident. Many listeners found him convincing.

Congress passed no law against the Klan after the hearings. The printed record, 184 pages from the Government Printing Office, survives today. It lets you set Simmons's *claims* beside the evidence the World gathered. Comparing a group's own story with outside evidence is one of the most important skills a historian has.

words.d: meetings where lawmakers question witnesses to gather facts
a brotherhood or lodge whose members share rituals and help one another
statements that something is true, which may need proof

look.title: Simmons Before the Committee
look.text: Simmons told the committee that the Klan was a patriotic fraternal order that obeyed the law. He denied that the organization had ordered the attacks reported in the press, and he asked the lawmakers to judge it by its stated ideals.
look.cite: U.S. House of Representatives, Committee on Rules, The Ku-Klux Klan: Hearings, 67th Congress, 1st Session (Government Printing Office, 1921)
look.prompt: Which evidence from the World series would you use to test Simmons's claims? What question would you have asked him?

check.q: Which committee held the 1921 hearings on the Klan?
check.why: The reading says the House Committee on Rules opened hearings on October 11, 1921.

check.q: How did Simmons describe the Klan?
choices: As a patriotic, law-abiding fraternal order
check.why: The reading says Simmons presented the Klan as a patriotic, law-abiding fraternal order.

check.q: What did Congress do after the hearings?
choices: It passed no law against the Klan
check.why: The reading says Congress passed no law against the Klan after the hearings.

lessons.title: Chicago's Unity League
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's American Unity League fought the Klan by printing members' names in its paper Tolerance, which raised hard questions.
reading: In 1922, people in Chicago formed the American Unity League. Most of its members were Roman Catholic. It set out to fight the Klan by breaking its secrecy. Its weekly paper, Tolerance, ran from 1922 into 1923. It printed the names, addresses and jobs of thousands of people it said were Klan members in the Chicago area.

The idea was simple. The Klan depended on secrecy. Its members wanted to keep their friends, customers and jobs while working against their neighbors. Once named in public, they had to face their community. This tactic is called *exposure*: making hidden facts public so people must answer for them.

Exposure is powerful, but it carries risks. A list can contain mistakes. Being named can bring threats or a lost job, whether the name is right or wrong. Today, publishing someone's private information so others can target them is called *doxxing*. People still debate where exposing a hate group ends and unfair harm begins. Your answer shows what you value about *privacy*.

words.d: making hidden facts public so people must answer for them
publishing someone's private information so that others can target them
a person's right to keep some information to themselves

look.prompt: Which list would you trust more, and why? Write two rules you would follow before printing any list of names.

check.why: The reading defines exposure as making hidden facts public so people must answer for them.

lessons.title: The Klan War in Williamson County
lessons.mainIdea: In southern Illinois, Klan-backed liquor raids set off a deadly local war in 1924 and 1925.
reading: Williamson County lies in the coal country of southern Illinois. In the 1920s, Prohibition made alcohol illegal, but a *bootlegger*, someone who makes or sells alcohol against the law, could still find buyers. Beginning in the winter of 1923 to 1924, the Klan backed a series of raids on bootleggers and saloons. A raider named S. Glenn Young led them.

The raids set off a local war. On one side were the Klan and its raiders. Critics called them a *vigilante* force, people taking the law into their own hands. On the other were the sheriff's allies and the Shelton gang of bootleggers. Gunfights broke out in the towns of Herrin and Marion. On January 24, 1925, a shootout in a Herrin cigar store killed four men: Young, Deputy Ora Thomas, and two of Young's companions.

Was it about liquor or about people? The Klan said it was enforcing the law. Critics point out that many of those raided were Italian immigrants and Catholics, groups the Klan attacked everywhere. Historians see more than one *motive* at work. Within a few years the local Klan had lost its power. Keep this separate from the Herrin Massacre of 1922, a deadly mine-strike clash that was not a Klan event.

words.d: a person who makes or sells alcohol against the law
a person who takes the law into his or her own hands without lawful authority
the reason a person or group does something

look.title: Liquor or Prejudice?
look.text: Claim 1: The raids were about enforcing Prohibition, which was the law of the land. Claim 2: The raids were about targeting immigrant and Catholic families the Klan already hated. Both claims were made in the 1920s. Both are still discussed by historians today.
look.prompt: What evidence would support each claim? Could both be partly true? Explain your thinking.

check.why: The reading says a raider named S. Glenn Young led the raids.

check.q: What happened in the Herrin cigar store on January 24, 1925?

check.why: The reading says a shootout there killed Young, Deputy Ora Thomas and two of Young's companions.

check.q: How is the Herrin Massacre of 1922 different from the Klan war?
choices: It was a mine-strike clash, not a Klan event
check.why: The reading says the Herrin Massacre of 1922 was a deadly mine-strike clash that was not a Klan event.

lessons.title: One Woman's Testimony
lessons.mainIdea: Madge Oberholtzer's dying declaration sent Indiana Klan leader D. C. Stephenson to prison for life.
reading: D. C. Stephenson led the Klan in Indiana in the early 1920s. His title was Grand Dragon. Indiana had one of the largest Klans in the nation. Stephenson had great political power, and many officials owed their elections to Klan votes. He presented himself as a champion of law, order and clean living.

In March 1925, Stephenson kidnapped a young woman named Madge Oberholtzer, who worked for the state of Indiana. He violently attacked her. She was badly hurt and died on April 14, 1925. Before she died, she gave a sworn statement about what he had done. A statement like this, made by a person who knows she is dying, is called a *dying declaration*.

The court allowed her statement as evidence. On November 14, 1925, a jury in Noblesville, Indiana, reached its *verdict*. It convicted Stephenson of second-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life in prison. He filed an *appeal*, but in 1932 the Indiana Supreme Court upheld the verdict. Her words broke the most powerful Klan leader in the North.

words.d: a sworn statement by a person who knows he or she is dying, which a court may accept as evidence
the decision a jury reaches at the end of a trial
a request for a higher court to review a trial's decision

look.title: The Court Upholds the Verdict
look.text: The Indiana Supreme Court upheld Stephenson's murder conviction. It ruled that Madge Oberholtzer's sworn statement, made when she knew she was dying, had been properly admitted as evidence at his trial.
look.cite: Stephenson v. State, 205 Ind. 141, 179 N.E. 633 (Indiana Supreme Court, 1932)
look.prompt: Courts usually want witnesses to speak in person. Why might they accept a dying declaration instead?

check.q: What is a dying declaration?
choices: A sworn statement by a person who knows she is dying
check.why: The reading defines a dying declaration as a statement made by a person who knows she is dying.

check.q: What was the verdict in Stephenson's trial?
choices: He was convicted of second-degree murder and sentenced to life
check.why: The reading says a jury in Noblesville convicted him of second-degree murder, and he was sentenced to life.

check.q: What was Stephenson's title in the Klan?
check.why: The reading says Stephenson led the Klan in Indiana with the title Grand Dragon.

lessons.title: The Fall of the Second Klan
lessons.mainIdea: Scandal, exposure and organized opposition drove the Klan's membership down sharply in the late 1920s.
reading: The Stephenson case shocked many Klan members. The Klan had sold itself as a defender of morals and law. Now its most powerful Northern leader was a convicted murderer. The *scandal*, a public event that causes shock and anger, drove members away. In Indiana they left in large numbers. Elsewhere, fights among leaders over money and power drove others out.

Opposition had been growing too. On May 17, 1924, students from the University of Notre Dame, a Catholic school, went into South Bend, Indiana, to *confront* a Klan rally. Catholic, Jewish and Black groups, newspapers and lawyers kept up the pressure. Across the country, neighbors organized to oppose Klan rallies and candidates.

Hiram Evans had replaced Simmons as the Klan's national leader in 1922. He could not stop the fall. By 1930 the Klan was a small shadow of what it had been only five years before. Exposure, courts and organized *civic groups* had broken the hold of a secret order that once counted its members in the millions.

words.d: a public event that causes shock and anger
to face someone or something directly, especially to oppose it
groups of citizens who work together for their community

look.title: Why Did It Fall?
look.text: Factor A: The Indiana leader is convicted of murder. Factor B: Newspapers print the Klan's fees, forms and members' names. Factor C: Students and neighbors confront Klan rallies. Factor D: Leaders fight each other over money and power.
look.prompt: Rank the four factors from most to least important in the Klan's collapse. Support your top choice with evidence from this chapter.

check.why: The reading says Notre Dame students went into South Bend on May 17, 1924, to confront a Klan rally.

check.why: The reading says Hiram Evans replaced Simmons as national leader in 1922.

check.q: Why did the Stephenson case hurt the Klan so badly?

check.why: The reading says the Klan sold itself as a defender of morals and law, but its top Northern leader was a convicted murderer.

lessons.title: Ida B. Wells: Facts as a Weapon
lessons.mainIdea: Ida B. Wells used white newspapers' own reports as data to expose the lies behind lynching, and she did it from Chicago.
reading: Ida B. Wells was born into slavery in Holly Springs, Mississippi, in 1862. She became a teacher and then a *journalist*, a person who reports the news, in Memphis, Tennessee. In 1892 a white mob in Memphis killed three Black businessmen. One of them was her friend. Their grocery store had competed with a white-owned store nearby.

Wells began to investigate *lynching*, the killing of a person by a mob without any trial. Many white newspapers claimed lynchings punished terrible crimes. Wells tested that claim. She collected the white newspapers' own reports and checked what the victims had actually been accused of. The claim often fell apart. After she wrote about it, threats kept her from returning to Memphis.

She settled in Chicago, married and raised a family there. In 1895 she published A Red Record in Chicago. It gathered lynching cases and counted them year by year. Her method was to use *data*, facts and numbers collected to answer a question, against a lie. She took part in founding the NAACP in 1909 and worked from Chicago for the rest of her life.

words.d: a person who gathers and reports the news
the killing of a person by a mob without any trial
facts and numbers collected to answer a question

look.title: Wells Explains Her Method
look.text: Wells told readers that her figures did not come from Black sources. She drew them from records kept by white newspapers, so no critic could say she had invented them. With those records she showed how often the crime used to excuse a lynching had not even been charged.
look.cite: Ida B. Wells, A Red Record (Chicago: Donohue and Henneberry, 1895)
look.prompt: Why was it smart to use her opponents' own newspapers? How does that choice make her argument stronger?

check.q: What is lynching?
choices: The killing of a person by a mob without any trial
check.why: The reading defines lynching as the killing of a person by a mob without any trial.

check.q: Where did Wells publish A Red Record in 1895?
check.why: The reading says Wells published A Red Record in Chicago in 1895.

check.q: What was Wells's method?
choices: She used white newspapers' own reports as data to test their claims
check.why: The reading says she collected white newspapers' own reports and checked what victims had actually been accused of.

lessons.title: The NAACP and Its Membership List
lessons.mainIdea: In NAACP v. Alabama (1958), the Supreme Court protected the NAACP's membership list from a state that wanted it.
reading: The NAACP was founded in 1909. It fought lynching and *segregation*, the forced separation of people by race, through courts, research and public pressure. In 1915 it led protests against The Birth of a Nation. Over the next decades, its lawyers won major civil rights cases before the Supreme Court.

In the 1950s, the state of Alabama tried to force the NAACP to hand over its membership lists. Members knew what could happen if their names became public. They could lose jobs, face threats or be attacked. The NAACP refused to give up the names. The case went to the U.S. Supreme Court as NAACP v. Alabama.

On June 30, 1958, the Court ruled *unanimously*, with every justice agreeing, for the NAACP. Justice Harlan wrote the opinion. Alabama could not force the group to reveal its members, because that would expose them to harm and weaken their *freedom of association*, the right to join with others for a shared cause. Notice the twist. A secret list can protect people, not only hide wrongdoing.

words.d: the forced separation of people by race
with every member agreeing
the right to join together with others for a shared cause

look.text: 1922: A Chicago paper prints the names of people it says belong to the Klan, to break a hate group's secrecy. 1958: The Supreme Court rules that Alabama cannot force the NAACP to reveal its members, to protect them from harm.
look.prompt: Both cases involve a list of members that someone wanted kept secret. What makes the two situations different? Try to write one rule that fits both.

lessons.title: Stetson Kennedy and the Debate
lessons.mainIdea: Stetson Kennedy's famous story of going undercover in the Klan was later shown to borrow from another informant, and it is still debated.
reading: Stetson Kennedy was a writer from Florida who fought the Klan in the 1940s. He said he went undercover inside the Georgia Klan in 1946 and 1947. He also said he passed its secret words to the makers of the Adventures of Superman radio show. In June 1946 the show aired a 16-episode story called Clan of the Fiery Cross. Young listeners heard Superman defeat a hate group.

The story became famous. In 2005 the best-selling book Freakonomics retold it. Then a researcher named Ben Green found problems. On January 8, 2006, the Freakonomics authors, Steven Levitt and Stephen Dubner, wrote an article called Hoodwinked? in the New York Times Magazine. They reported that much of Kennedy's inside information had come from an *informant* known as John Brown.

Kennedy's defenders answer that he did real, brave work against the Klan. The Superman series is not in doubt. Neither is Georgia's 1947 move to revoke the Klan's state charter. What is still debated is how much Kennedy chose to *embellish*, or add to, his own role. A *memoir* can be both useful and unreliable. Checking it against other records is the historian's job.

words.d: a person who secretly gives information about a group to someone outside it
to add details to a story to make it more exciting, sometimes untrue ones
a person's written account of his or her own life and experiences

look.title: The Authors Correct Themselves
look.text: Levitt and Dubner wrote that Kennedy's own papers showed that much of the inside information he described had come from another man working inside the Klan. They reported this as a correction to the version of the story they had told in their book.
look.cite: Steven D. Levitt and Stephen J. Dubner, Hoodwinked?, New York Times Magazine, January 8, 2006
look.prompt: Why is it unusual, and valuable, when authors publicly correct a story they told? What does it teach about checking sources?

check.q: What was Clan of the Fiery Cross?

check.why: The reading says the Adventures of Superman radio show aired this 16-episode story in June 1946.

check.why: The reading says Levitt and Dubner reported that much of Kennedy's information came from an informant known as John Brown.

check.q: What does embellish mean?
choices: To add details to a story to make it more exciting
check.why: The reading defines embellish as adding to a story, here Kennedy's own role.

review.q: How did Ida B. Wells prove that claims about lynching were false?
choices: She used white newspapers' own reports as data
review.why: Wells gathered white newspapers' reports and checked what victims had actually been accused of.

review.q: How do the Tolerance lists and NAACP v. Alabama differ?
choices: Both were decided by the Supreme Court
Tolerance exposed a hate group's members; the Court protected a civil rights group's members
review.why: Tolerance printed names to break the Klan's secrecy, while the 1958 ruling kept NAACP members' names private to protect them.

review.q: Why is Stetson Kennedy's story still debated?
choices: No one knows if the Klan existed in Georgia
Kennedy denied ever writing about the Klan
Much of his inside information came from an informant, and how much he embellished is disputed
review.why: The 2006 article reported an informant was the source of much of his information, while his defenders point to his real anti-Klan work.
